analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to offer basic health coverage and creates state plans for people insurers reject.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 1990, the bill never got a markup or vote in any House committee and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required nearly every employer to offer workers a basic health plan or a payroll-deduction plan, and to set up state-run nonprofit health systems covering anyone insurers turn away as uninsurable or penalize for preexisting conditions. It would have made insurance cheaper by wiping out state laws that require specific benefits and state rules restricting managed care, letting multiple-employer plans operate tax-free, and raising the self-employed health insurance deduction from 25% to 100%. It was a market-based universal coverage framework: coverage would flow almost entirely through employers and private plans, with state systems as a backup.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured workers and their families would have gained a guaranteed offer of coverage from their employer or access to a state system. People with preexisting conditions whom insurers reject would have had a guaranteed place to buy coverage. Self-employed people would have kept far more of their health insurance costs tax-free, and states would have received federal grants to build their systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured workers and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Every employer except brand-new firms and those with two or fewer workers would have had to offer each uncovered employee either a basic group health plan or a group health payroll deduction plan.

State health benefits systems would have had to cover individuals rejected as uninsurable risks and provide coverage for material preexisting conditions, ending the situation where sick people simply could not buy insurance at all.
The deduction for health insurance costs of self-employed individuals would have risen from 25% to 100% and become permanent.
HHS would have run a grant program, authorized at $200 million per year for fiscal 1991-1993, to help states and alternative systems stand up universal coverage.

Multiple employer welfare arrangements (MEWAs) offering basic benefits would have gotten tax-exempt status without the usual common-employer restrictions, letting small businesses band together to buy coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would have borne a new obligation to offer coverage, though they could satisfy it with a plan employees pay for out of their own wages. States would have had to build and regulate new nonprofit health systems. Taxpayers would have funded the grant program and the cost of the larger self-employed deduction. Consumers would have paid in another way: state laws requiring insurers to cover specific benefits and state rules reining in managed care would have been wiped out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, taxpayers, and state-protected benefit mandates

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws that mandate specific health benefits and state laws restricting managed care, so consumers would have lost state-required protections — maternity care, specific provider coverage, and limits on rate-setting or utilization review — in exchange for cheaper, thinner basic plans.

An employer could satisfy the mandate simply by offering a payroll deduction plan funded entirely by the employee's own wages, so the guarantee was an offer of coverage, not affordable coverage; the bill imposed no employer contribution requirement for most workers.

The content of 'basic health benefits' would have been set by HHS regulations written years later, and state systems could offer a catastrophic-only option, so the floor could have been minimal and cost-sharing high.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a genuine path to universal access — a coverage offer for every worker and a guaranteed market for people insurers refuse to cover — which was the central health policy problem of 1990. But it bought affordability by stripping state benefit mandates and managed-care rules, allowed employers to shift premium costs entirely onto workers, and left the actual benefit package to later regulation. It was a framework bill, not a finished guarantee: its value depended heavily on how HHS wrote the rules and how states responded.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then parked in four subcommittees in the spring of 1990, and none of them ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Fred Grandy of Iowa introduced the bill on February 22, 1990, joined by two Republican cosponsors.

The bill was referred the same day to the Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce committees — jurisdiction was split because it touched labor law, taxes, and health programs at once.
Between March 6 and April 4, 1990, the three committees referred it to their health and labor subcommittees, a step from which most bills never return.
No subcommittee or full committee ever held a markup or vote, and no floor action followed; the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers faced no new coverage obligations or federal rules, and the uninsured — including people uninsurable for preexisting conditions — remained without a coverage guarantee. Status quo interests were better off because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers; the uninsured stayed uncovered

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill died quietly in committees chaired by Democrats; no vote was ever taken, so no formal party split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer-based benefit plans
industries.note: The bill makes private employer-based group coverage the permanent channel for universal access, with state systems only as a backstop, and gives multiple-employer plans tax-exempt status and lighter reporting. Insurers gain a mandated market and regulatory relief, while consumers get coverage whose depth depends on plan design they do not control.

The bill preempts state laws restricting managed care — rate negotiation, provider limits, utilization review — letting plans control costs with fewer state constraints. Cost control can benefit premiums, but it removes state-level checks on how plans restrict care.

Employers face a new obligation to offer basic coverage, but firms with two or fewer workers are exempt and any employer can satisfy the mandate with a plan employees pay for themselves. Preempting state benefit mandates lowers the cost of whatever plan they offer.

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and small business owners
industries.note: The self-employed health insurance deduction jumps from 25% to 100% and is made permanent, a tax benefit concentrated among higher-income independent workers.
States would receive grants of up to $200 million a year for fiscal 1991-1993 and a federal framework for state nonprofit health systems covering uninsurable and preexisting-condition cases.
